# On the Peculiar Art of Noticing

I want to talk about noticing, that simple act we perform thousands of times daily without acknowledgment or ceremony. We notice that our coffee has cooled. We notice a friend's tone has shifted mid-conversation. We notice the way light falls through a window at 4 PM in October, different than it does in June. These moments pass through our consciousness like water through open fingers, and we rarely pause to consider their strange significance.

There's something almost magical about noticing that deserves more attention than it receives. It sits at the intersection of perception and consciousness, of the world and our mind's engagement with it. When we notice something, we're performing an act of creation, in a sense. The coffee's coolness doesn't announce itself—we determine it's cooled. The light's quality isn't inherently meaningful—we find meaning in it. Noticing is the mechanism by which raw experience becomes material for our inner lives.

I became obsessed with this concept recently while sitting in a waiting room. You know the experience: fluorescent lights, outdated magazines, the particular smell that seems to exist in no other environment on Earth. My appointment was running late, and I found myself with that rare commodity in modern life—truly unstructured time. No phone task presenting itself as urgent. No book to hide behind. Just observation.

I noticed the woman across from me had been reading the same page of her magazine for twelve minutes. I noticed the receptionist's practiced smile, which differed subtly from her genuine smile when she spoke to a colleague. I noticed the small potted plant in the corner, struggling in the artificial light, and felt a pang of something I can't quite name—identification, perhaps. I noticed that my noticing was making time pass more interestingly than any distraction could.

This is something we've lost, I think. The capacity to notice without immediately processing, without moving toward action or judgment. We're trained to notice things only insofar as they're relevant to our goals. We notice the traffic light because we need to drive. We notice the typo in the email because we need to send it correctly. We notice our partner's sadness because we care and want to help. All of this is good and necessary, but it's also a kind of truncated noticing.

There's a deeper form of noticing that operates without purpose. It's the noticing that artists and writers and certain kinds of people seem to be wired for. They notice the way an elderly man's hands shake slightly, not to diagnose or to fix, but because there's something in that tremor—the visible evidence of age, of a nervous system firing differently now than it did decades ago—that arrests their attention. They notice how a child pronounces a word incorrectly in a way that's somehow more logical than the correct pronunciation, revealing the beautiful rules children intuit about language. They notice the color of rust, the particular sadness of an empty playground, the comedy of a pigeon's iridescent neck catching the light as it waddles.

These noticing-people are sometimes dismissed as overly sensitive or impractical. "Don't you have things to do?" I imagine people saying to them as they stand transfixed, staring at nothing in particular. And yes, probably they do have things to do. But they're engaged in something I've come to believe is deeply important: the work of actually living in the world rather than just passing through it.

Consider how we talk about time. We say time passes, like it's something happening to us rather than something we're living. But time isn't something that passes—moments are. And our relationship with those moments depends entirely on whether we notice them. Two people can experience the exact same hour. One can describe it as time wasted, time that flew by, time killed. The other can describe it as filled with small discoveries, quiet pleasures, interesting details. The only difference is noticing.

I wonder if this is why depression and anxiety are so prevalent in our current moment. We've built a world that's antithetical to noticing. Everything is designed to grab our attention and direct it toward consumption or productivity. Our phones interrupt constantly, training us to have fractured attention. Our workdays are scheduled to the minute. Our entertainment is optimized to be maximally engaging. There's no space for the quiet noticing that human consciousness seems to crave.

When I look at children, before they're fully socialized, I see remarkable noticers. They stop dead in their tracks to examine an ant. They notice the texture of tree bark. They notice when an adult is pretending to listen versus actually listening. They notice inconsistencies and call them out with the brutal honesty of someone who hasn't yet learned which things we're supposed to pretend not to see. Then we train this out of them. We teach them to be productive, goal-oriented, efficient. We don't mean to diminish their capacity for noticing—we're just trying to help them succeed in the world as it is.

But what if we're wrong about what success means? What if the capacity to notice deeply is actually more valuable, more foundational to wellbeing, than the ability to achieve goals efficiently?

There's a practice in Zen Buddhism called shikantaza, sometimes translated as "just sitting." It's meditation without an object, without trying to achieve any particular state. You just sit and notice. Everything that arises in consciousness is treated with equal attention—thoughts, sensations, sounds, the feeling of breath. It's deceptively simple and remarkably difficult. The mind rebels against it. It wants to be doing something, achieving something, progressing toward something. The idea of noticing without agenda feels foreign and uncomfortable.

I tried this recently, seriously tried it, sitting for twenty minutes with no goal other than to notice. The first five minutes were torment. My mind kept generating urgent tasks I should be doing, worries I should be addressing, ways I was wasting my time. The next ten minutes were abstract and dreamy, my attention drifting. But in the last five minutes, something shifted. I stopped fighting the restlessness and simply noticed it. I noticed the particular quality of boredom that arises when the mind isn't fed stimulation. I noticed how that boredom has a strange texture—not entirely unpleasant once you stop resisting it. I noticed the sound of my neighbor's television through the wall, the slight ache in my lower back, the way my breath naturally deepens when I stop monitoring it. And I noticed that in noticing, time had become rich again. Twenty minutes had contained the texture and detail of much longer.

This might sound like I'm advocating for some kind of retreat from the world, and I'm not. The world needs people who are focused and productive and goal-oriented. We need engineers and project managers and people who are good at executing on plans. But we also need people who notice, and we need to cultivate the capacity for noticing in ourselves even if our roles don't require it.

I think about writers I admire and what they have in common. It's not always talent, though that helps. It's not always formal training. It's usually a commitment to noticing. The best writers are the ones who've been paying attention to how people actually talk, how light actually moves, how small moments contain strange truths. They've been noticing the world in a way that's not driven by immediate usefulness.

The same is probably true of the best parents, the best friends, the best craftspeople. They notice things. They notice when someone's smile doesn't reach their eyes. They notice the way their child approaches a problem differently than they expected. They notice when their hands have learned something new through repetition. They notice when the wood they're working with has a particular grain that suggests what shape it wants to become.

There's something almost mystical about this last kind of noticing—the kind where you notice what something wants to be. Michelangelo talked about this with marble, said he could see the figure inside the stone and was just revealing it. A master gardener notices what the soil wants to grow. A good teacher notices what a student is ready to learn. This kind of noticing requires patience and attention and a surrender of complete control. You have to notice and respond rather than impose.

I wonder if this is why so much modern work feels hollow. So much of it requires that we not notice—that we implement strategies designed by people we don't know for outcomes we didn't choose for customers we don't meet. We're explicitly told not to notice the ways our work might be harmful or inefficient or contrary to human wellbeing. We're trained to ignore our own noticing and trust the system instead.

The antidote isn't to quit working or to retreat entirely, but to find places in life where we can practice noticing without agenda. It might be a hobby. It might be a few minutes in the morning before the day begins. It might be a deliberate walk where the point is just to notice, not to exercise or get somewhere.

I've been experimenting with this. I take walks where I'm explicitly not trying to get anywhere or accomplish anything. I just notice what's there. The way a building's brick has settled unevenly after decades. The names people have given to their businesses and what you can infer about them from those choices. The exact color of a particular dog's fur. The way different people move through the world—some hurried, some flowing, some rigid, some loose.

These walks don't make me more productive. They don't accomplish anything by conventional standards. But they make me feel more alive. There's something that happens to consciousness when it's freed from the demand to achieve and allowed to simply perceive. The world becomes more vivid. Time becomes richer. I remember why I wanted to be alive in the first place.

I think about my younger self, before I was fully trained into productivity. I remember noticing things constantly. I remember being fascinated by minutiae. I remember that this fascination felt like one of the few unambiguously good things about being alive. It didn't need justification. The fact that I could notice the world was its own reward.

Somewhere in becoming an adult, I forgot that. I got very efficient at noticing only what was relevant. I became a focused instrument directed at various goals. And I got things done, accomplished things I was supposed to accomplish, achieved a reasonable version of success. But something was lost, and it wasn't until recently that I realized what it was.

The practice of noticing, of giving attention freely to the world without demanding it produce something valuable, might be the most human thing we can do. It's what separates existence from life. It's what makes consciousness more than just a mechanism for survival and reproduction. When we notice, when we pay real attention, we're saying yes to existence. We're saying that this moment matters, that these details matter, that the world is worth our careful attention even if we never do anything with what we notice.

And maybe, eventually, we do something with it. Maybe we write it down or draw it or work it into something we make. Or maybe we don't. Maybe we just live more fully, more consciously, because we've noticed. Maybe that's enough.

The waiting room experience I mentioned has stayed with me. I've started going back to that practice of just noticing, without the pressure of productivity attached. Some days it feels pointless. My mind resists. I feel I should be doing something more important. But I keep returning to it, and each time I do, I'm reminded of something I'd forgotten: that attention itself is a form of love. When you notice someone or something, you're saying it's worth your attention. You're saying it exists and matters.

In a world that's increasingly hostile to such noticing—faster, more demanding, more fragmented—I think this practice becomes more necessary. Not as a retreat but as a form of resistance. A quiet insistence that some things matter not because they're productive but because they're real, because they're here, because we're conscious enough to perceive them.

So I'll keep noticing. The way morning light changes through November. The kindness of a stranger's unnecessary smile. The feel of a well-made pen in my hand. The improbable survival of that struggling plant in the waiting room. The small details that make a life feel like it's worth the living.
